summary: Defines the Management Information Base objects used to manage version 2 of the OSPF routing protocol, which works with IPv4. OSPF version 3 is handled separately.

plainLanguage.summary: A router that speaks OSPF can tell a management system almost anything about its state, but only if both sides agree on the names of the values to exchange. This document fixes those names. It defines a MIB, the shared catalogue of values that SNMP reads, covering the areas, interfaces, neighbours and link state advertisements of an OSPF version 2 router.

questions: how to monitor ospf with snmp
how do i enable ospf with snmp
subtitle: The standard objects a management system reads to see and control OSPF version 2.

tldr.problem: OSPF version 2 has many features and settings, and operators need a standard way to read and change them on routers from different vendors.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the OSPF-MIB module, rooted at mib-2 14, a set of tables and variables for areas, interfaces, neighbours and the link state database, plus an optional OSPF-TRAP-MIB module of notifications.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1850 while staying backwards compatible, and adds support for NSSAs, Opaque LSAs, graceful restart and stub routers. OSPF version 3 is not covered.

today: RFC 4750 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2006. It obsoletes RFC 1850 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard catalogue of OSPF version 2 objects for SNMP. OSPF version 3 has its own MIB and is not covered here.

sections.title: The Management Framework
sections.content:
Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, or MIB. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), and the objects are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information. This memo specifies a MIB module compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The module covers version 2 of the Open Shortest Path First routing protocol, which is specific to the IPv4 address family. Version 3 of OSPF is specific to IPv6 and is not covered here.

For the benefit of row creation in conceptual tables, DEFVAL clauses give default values that an agent should use for instances of variables that need to be created because of a Set-Request but are not specified in it. For objects that are read-only and have no DEFVAL clause, the implied value is zero, and those objects are of the SYNTAX Counter32 or Gauge32. Where no default exists, the Robustness Principle applies: management stations should include as many columnar objects as possible, for example all read-write objects, in a Set-Request that creates a conceptual row, and agents should accept a Set-Request with as few of those objects as they need.

The MIB defines several counters: ospfOriginateNewLsas and ospfRxNewLsas in the general group, ospfSpfRuns and ospfAreaNssaTranslatorEvents in the area table, ospfIfEvents in the interface table, ospfVirtIfEvents in the virtual interface table, ospfNbrEvents in the neighbour table and ospfVirtNbrEvents in the virtual neighbour table. As a best practice, a management entity reading these counters should use the discontinuity object, ospfDiscontinuityTime, to see whether an event that would invalidate its understanding of the counters has occurred; a restart of the OSPF routing process is a possible example.

SNMPv3 supports contexts, which can be used to implement MIB views on multiple OSPF instances on the same system.
sections.plainLanguage: A management system reads a router's state through SNMP, and the names of the values it reads have to be agreed in advance. This document is that agreement: a catalogue of the values a router exposes about OSPF. It also says how a new row in one of the catalogues should be filled in, so that a management system and a router do not disagree about defaults.

sections.title: The Default Configuration
sections.content:
OSPF is a powerful routing protocol, equipped with features to handle virtually any configuration requirement that might reasonably be found within an Autonomous System. With that power comes a fair degree of complexity, which the sheer number of objects in the MIB will attest to. Care has therefore been taken to define default values for virtually every object, to minimize the amount of parameterization required in the typical case.

The assumptions are that IP has already been configured, that the ifTable has already been configured, that ifSpeed is estimated by the interface drivers, that the OSPF process automatically discovers all IP interfaces and creates corresponding OSPF interfaces, and that the OSPF process automatically creates the areas required for those interfaces.

On those assumptions the simplest configuration of an OSPF process requires only that the process be enabled, which can be accomplished with a single SET of ospfAdminStat to enabled. The configured system then has a Router ID that is one of the IP addresses of the device, is neither an Area Border Router nor an Autonomous System Border Router, has every IP interface as an OSPF interface whether or not it carries an address, puts each interface in area 0.0.0.0, the backbone, and has authentication disabled.

All broadcast and point-to-point interfaces are then operational, while non-broadcast multi-access interfaces require the configuration of at least one neighbour. The timers on all direct interfaces are a Hello interval of 10 seconds, a dead timeout of 40 seconds, a retransmission interval of 5 seconds, a transit delay of 1 second and a poll interval of 120 seconds. No direct links to hosts are configured, no addresses are summarized, metrics are unambiguous and intelligent, and no virtual links are configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The document works out what an OSPF router looks like if nobody configures anything. It turns out that one setting is enough to start the process, and everything else follows: every interface joins the backbone area, no authentication is used, and the timers take standard values.

sections.title: The Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The MIB is composed of the General Variables, the Area Data Structure, the Area Stub Metric Table, the Link State Database, the Address Range Table, the Host Table, the Interface Table, the Interface Metric Table, the Virtual Interface Table, the Neighbor Table, the Virtual Neighbor Table, the External Link State Database, the Aggregate Range Table, the Local Link State Database and the AS-scope Link State Database. It supports the base OSPFv2 specification and extensions to OSPFv2 such as RFC 1765, RFC 1793, RFC 2370, RFC 3101 and RFC 3623. A separate MIB for notifications, the traps, exists and is entirely optional.

Each section has a purpose. The general variables describe what is global to the OSPF process. The area data structure describes all of the areas the router takes part in, and the area table includes data for Not-So-Stubby-Area translation, while the area stub metric table describes the metrics advertised into a stub area by the default router. The link state database is provided primarily to give detailed information for network debugging, and the address range table and host table are provided to view configured network summary and host route information.

The interface table and the interface metric table together describe the various IP interfaces known to OSPF. The metrics are placed in a separate table in order to simplify dealing with multiple types of service, and the interface table includes link-local Opaque type-9 link state advertisement statistics. The virtual interface table describes virtual links to the OSPF process, in the same way, and the neighbour table and the virtual neighbour table describe the neighbours.

The local link state database table and the virtual local link state database table are identical in format to the main link state database table but contain only link-local Opaque type-9 advertisements, and the AS-scope table contains only AS-scoped advertisements. The area LSA count table maintains the number of link state advertisements on a per-area, per-LSA-type basis.
sections.plainLanguage: The catalogue is split into one table for each thing an OSPF router knows about: its areas, its interfaces, its neighbours, and the link state advertisements it has received. Some tables exist only to make debugging easier.

sections.title: The OSPF MIB Module
sections.content:
The module is rooted at { mib-2 14 }. It defines textual conventions for the values it uses: the Area ID, which has the format of an IP address but the function of defining a summarization point for link state advertisements; the Router ID, which also has the format of an IP address but identifies the router independently of its IP addresses; the internal metric, an unsigned value up to 0xFFFF; the external metric, up to 0xFFFFFF; a Status of enabled or disabled; a positive integer; the range of intervals in seconds on which Hello messages are exchanged; and the values in seconds that are bounded by the maximum age of an LSA.

The general group holds the objects that apply to the whole process, among them ospfRouterId, ospfAdminStat, ospfRFC1583Compatibility, ospfReferenceBandwidth and ospfDiscontinuityTime. The rest of the module is a set of tables, each indexed by the values that identify a row.

The area table is indexed by the area ID and holds the authentication type, the external import setting, the number of shortest path first runs, the counts of area border and autonomous system border routers, the number of link state advertisements and their checksum sum, the area summary, and the NSSA translator role, state, stability interval and event count. The link state database table is indexed by the area ID, the LSA type, the link state ID and the router ID. The interface table is indexed by the interface IP address and the address-less interface index, and holds the area, the interface type, the administrative status, the router priority, the transit delay, the retransmit, hello, dead and poll intervals, the interface state, the designated and backup designated routers, the event counter, the authentication key and type, and the LSA count and checksum sum. The neighbour table is indexed by the neighbour IP address and the address-less interface index, and holds the neighbour's router ID, options, priority, state, event count and the length of the link state retransmission queue.
sections.plainLanguage: Every table is keyed by the values that identify one row, usually an address and an index. The module also defines the vocabulary the values use, so that an area ID, a router ID and a metric all have one agreed meaning.

sections.title: Trap Overview
sections.content:
OSPF is an event-driven routing protocol, where an event can be a change in an OSPF interface's link-level status, the expiration of an OSPF timer, or the reception of an OSPF protocol packet. Many of the actions that OSPF takes as a result of these events will change the routing topology. As routing topologies become large and complex, it is often difficult to locate the source of a topology change or an unpredicted routing path by polling a large number of routers. Because of the difficulty of polling a large number of devices, a more prudent approach is for devices to notify a network manager of potentially critical OSPF events using SNMP traps. The traps are an optional but very useful extension to the OSPF MIB.

The mechanism is straightforward. When an exception event occurs, the application notifies the local agent, which sends a trap to the appropriate SNMP management stations. The message includes the trap type and may include a list of trap-specific variables. The Router ID of the originator of the trap is included in the variable list so that the network manager may easily determine the source of the trap.

Four mechanisms keep the trap rate down. First, a router should not originate the expected interface-related traps until two of that interface's dead timer intervals have elapsed, because most critical events occur while OSPF is being enabled and those events are expected. The expected traps are ospfIfStateChange, ospfVirtIfStateChange, ospfNbrStateChange, ospfVirtNbrStateChange, ospfTxRetransmit and ospfVirtIfTxRetransmit, and the ospfMaxAgeLsa and ospfOriginateLsa traps wait for two dead intervals of the smallest dead timer.

Second, the traps are throttled with a sliding window, defined in seconds, and an upper bound on the number of traps generated within it. One window throttles all trap types except ospfLsdbOverflow and ospfLsdbApproachingOverflow, which are not throttled. The document suggests appropriate values of seven traps with a window time of ten seconds. Third, OSPF should generate at most one trap per OSPF event, with only the variables of the first unusual condition included, so that a packet holding several problems raises one trap rather than several. Fourth, a manager can poll the generalized event counters and enable specific OSPF traps when a particular counter starts increasing abnormally.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that sends a trap for every event would drown the manager, so the document sets four rules: stay quiet while the protocol is still starting up, cap the number of traps per time window, raise only one trap per event even if the event reveals several problems, and let the manager watch the counters and turn traps on only when something looks wrong.

sections.title: The Trap Definitions and the Translation Rules
sections.content:
The separate OSPF-TRAP-MIB defines twenty notifications. They cover virtual interface and virtual neighbour state changes, neighbour state changes, interface and virtual interface configuration errors, authentication failures, the reception of bad packets, retransmissions, the origination of an LSA, an LSA reaching maximum age, link state database overflow and approaching overflow, interface state changes, the NSSA translator status change, and the graceful restart status changes for the router, for a neighbour and for a virtual neighbour.

The definitions of the OSPF notifications pre-date the RFC 2578 requirement of having a zero value for the penultimate sub-identifier when translating SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 trap parameters to SNMPv1 trap parameters. RFC 3584 defines translation rules that intermediate proxy agents or multi-lingual agents can implement to convert notifications to SNMPv1 and back. Translating from SNMPv1 to SNMPv2 or SNMPv3 results in the SNMPv2 or SNMPv3 trap OID being the concatenation of the SNMPv1 enterprise parameter and two additional sub-identifiers, a zero and the SNMPv1 specific-trap parameter. Translating the other way, as the notifications are defined here, results in the SNMPv1 enterprise parameter being set to the SNMPv2 or SNMPv3 trap OID with the last sub-identifier removed, and the specific-trap parameter being set to that last sub-identifier. The conversion is not reversible, and a notification that originated from an SNMPv1 agent does not become the same notification as one from a native SNMPv2 or SNMPv3 agent.

The MIB modules that this document updates were originally written in SMIv1 for SNMPv1, when only traps were used. Because this version is written in SMIv2, it should be understood that all types of notification, trap and inform PDUs, may be used by native SNMPv2 and SNMPv3 agents, although only traps are mentioned. For backwards compatibility, the OSPF Trap module remains rooted at { ospf 16 }.
sections.plainLanguage: The document defines twenty kinds of trap, one for each event a manager might want to hear about. It also explains how a trap written in the newer SNMP versions is converted to the old SNMPv1 form, and warns that the conversion does not survive a round trip.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are a number of management objects defined in this MIB that have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

It is recommended that attention be given specifically to implementing the MAX-ACCESS clause in a number of objects, including ospfIfAuthKey, ospfIfAuthType, ospfVirtIfAuthKey and ospfVirtIfAuthType, in scenarios that do not use SNMPv3 strong security, that is, authentication and encryption. Extreme caution must be used to minimize the risk of cascading security vulnerabilities when SNMPv3 strong security is not used. When it is not used, these objects should have access of read-only, not read-create.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPsec, there is still no control over who on the secure network is allowed to GET or SET the objects in this MIB. It is recommended that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model of RFC 3414 and the View-based Access Control Model of RFC 3415. It is then a user responsibility to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB is properly configured to give access to the objects only to those principals that have a legitimate right to read or change them.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the objects in this catalogue let a manager change the router, including the authentication keys. The document says to make those read-only unless SNMPv3 security is in use, and to use SNMPv3's access control so that only the right people can change anything.

sections.title: Registration and Changes from RFC 1850
sections.content:
The MIB module in this document uses the IANA-assigned OBJECT IDENTIFIER value { mib-2 14 } from the SMI Numbers registry.

Appendix B records the differences from RFC 1850. The general group gained ospfRFC1583Compatibility, which indicates support for RFC 1583 compatibility and has a default of enabled, ospfReferenceBandwidth, which allows a reference bandwidth to be configured for the calculation of default interface metrics, and ospfDiscontinuityTime, which lets a management entity detect counter discontinuity events. Objects were added for graceful restart, namely ospfRestartSupport, ospfRestartInterval, ospfRestartAge, ospfRestartStrictLsaChecking and ospfRestartExitReason, and for stub routers, namely ospfStubRouterSupport and ospfStubRouteAdvertisement.

The area table gained the NSSA translator objects: ospfAreaNssaTranslatorRole for the configured role, ospfAreaNssaTranslatorState for the current role, ospfAreaNssaTranslatorStabilityInterval for how long to keep the current translation status, and ospfAreaNssaTranslatorEvents for the number of times the translation state has changed. The aggregate range table gained ospfAreaAggregateExtRouteTag, and a new trap, ospfNssaTranslatorStatusChange, was added.

Support for Opaque LSAs was added with ospfOpaqueLsaSupport and two new tables, ospfLocalLsdbTable for link-local type-9 advertisements and ospfVirtLocalLsdbTable for the same on virtual links. Each holds the LSA sequence, age and checksum, and the entire advertisement. An area LSA counter table was added, along with a section describing the translation of notification parameters between SNMP versions, an object group holding obsolete object groups, and the deprecation of ospfExtLsdbTable.
sections.plainLanguage: The catalogue keeps the name it had before, so existing management software still works. What changed is the content: objects for graceful restart, for stub routers, for opaque advertisements and for not-so-stubby areas were added, and the trap module gained a few more kinds of notification.

viz.caption: THE SECTIONS OF THE OSPF MIB (RFC 4750 SECTION 2)
THE DEFAULT TIMERS ON DIRECT INTERFACES
THE FOUR WAYS TO KEEP THE TRAP RATE DOWN

items.title: Ignore initial activity
items.text: Hold back the expected interface traps until two dead timer intervals have passed.

items.title: Throttle traps
items.text: A sliding window with an upper bound; seven traps in ten seconds is suggested.

items.title: One trap per event
items.text: Only the first unusual condition in an event raises a trap, with only its variables.

items.title: Poll event counters
items.text: A manager can watch the counters and enable specific traps when one starts rising abnormally.
